hello.note: Literally a term of respect ('I honor you'); the all-purpose Sepedi greeting for any time of day. The radio station Thobela FM, named for this word, broadcasts to Sepedi speakers nationwide.

good_morning.note: Built from Thobela plus mesong, 'in the morning'.

good_evening.note: Same pattern with mantšiboa, 'evening'; š is pronounced like English 'sh'.

goodbye.note: Literally 'stay well'; said by the one leaving. The one staying replies Sepela gabotse (seh-PEH-lah gah-BOH-tseh), 'go well'.

how_are_you.note: Literally 'where are you (all)?'; used as the everyday greeting regardless of how many people you're addressing. Northern Sotho phrasebooks pair this with the singular O kae? (oh KAH-eh), same literal 'where are you' pattern; some speakers instead ask O bjang? (oh BJAHNG), 'how (are) you', the construction more typical of Southern Sotho and Tswana.

youre_welcome.note: Literally 'you are received/welcomed', the passive of amogela 'to receive'; dictionaries give this specifically for the thanks-reply sense (distinct from the plural le amogetšwe used to welcome a guest), but independent examples of it spoken in that exact context are scarce, so treat it as a well-formed candidate rather than a confirmed one. Also plausible, on the pattern of neighboring Nguni languages that answer thanks with 'it's fine' rather than a 'welcome' word: Go lokile ('it's fine/alright') or Ga se selo ('it's nothing').

no_problem.note: Literally 'there is no problem/trouble'; casual, for brushing off a favor or small mishap. Also heard as Ga go na bothata (gah goh nah boh-TAH-tah). Bothata itself is pan-Sotho vocabulary (documented for Southern Sotho; Sepedi-specific dictionaries are too thin to confirm it independently), but it is the term Sepedi speakers are recorded using here. Go lokile ('it's fine') covers this same slot for many speakers, overlapping with the you're-welcome reply.

please.note: A softening particle tacked onto a request, e.g. Nthuše, hle ('help me, please'). To lead with 'please' up front, speakers instead open with Ke kgopela ('I request'), as in Ke kgopela meetse, 'please, water'.

excuse_me.note: Literally 'pardon/forgiveness'; used both to get someone's attention and to say sorry for a small bump. Some phrasebooks instead give the imperative Ntshwarele (n-tshwah-REH-leh), 'forgive me', for this slot.

sorry.note: Literally 'I have sadness/regret'; the fuller apology for a real mistake.

of_course.note: Literally 'in truth/certainly'; a firm, emphatic yes to a request. Nnete ('truth') is shared Sotho-Tswana vocabulary (well documented for Southern Sotho; Sepedi-specific references are thinner), but dictionaries consistently return ka nnete for 'of course/certainly/definitely' in Sepedi too. Ee, go bjalo ('yes, that's how it is') is a plausible looser alternative for agreeing readily.

amazing.note: From -makatša, 'to astonish'; a warm exclamation for something that blew you away. Flagged low-confidence: checked the other direction, makatšago on its own can also gloss as 'weird/strange', since astonishing can read as good or bad without context, so lean on tone of voice when using it.

delicious.note: Also just means 'nice/pleasant'; the everyday compliment for a cook.

cheers.note: From -thabiša, 'to bring joy'; said raising a glass. There is no literal Sepedi 'clink' word, so this fills in for the Western toast. Adding the present-tense a (Go a thabiša) shifts it to a full sentence, 'that's good', so it's left off here.
